summary: Details IETF policies on rights in Contributions, designed so that contributions can be made available to the IETF and Internet communities while letting authors keep as many rights as possible. It was replaced by RFC 5378.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a document to the IETF counts as agreeing to let the IETF publish it, translate it, and make revised versions of it, and as saying that the information in it is not confidential. The author keeps every other right. RFC 3978 spells out exactly what is granted, what the author promises, and what every published document must carry.

questions: what rights do ietf authors grant
what rights does an ietf author grant
subtitle: What an author gives up when they send a document to the IETF, and what they keep.

tldr.problem: The IETF needs the right to publish and to update the documents people send it, but most authors would rather keep as much of their copyright as possible.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists the rights every contributor grants when submitting, the representations they make about having the authority to grant them, and the exact notices that must appear in every IETF document.
tldr.outcome: It was Best Current Practice 78 from March 2005 and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 5378, so the current statement of these policies is in that document. RFC 4748 updates part of it.

today: RFC 3978, Best Current Practice 78, was obsoleted in 2010 by RFC 5378, which is the current statement of the IETF's policies on rights in contributions, and it was updated by RFC 4748. The rules described here are the ones that were in force from March 2005 until that replacement.

sections.title: Definitions and Purpose
sections.content:
Under the laws of most countries and current international treaties, for example the Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Work, authors obtain numerous rights in the works they produce automatically upon producing them. These rights include copyrights, moral rights and other rights. In many cases, if the author produces a work within the scope of their employment, most of those rights are usually assigned to the employer, either by operation of law or, in many cases, under contract. The Berne Convention names some rights as inalienable, meaning the author retains them in all cases.

RFC 3978 details the rights that the IETF requires in IETF Contributions, and the rights the IETF, as publisher of Internet-Drafts, requires in all such Drafts including RFC Editor Contributions. The RFC Editor may also define additional rights required for RFC Editor Contributions. The memo explains that these necessary rights and representations had until then been laid out in Section 10 of RFC 2026, and that in the years since that document was published the exact intent of that section had been the subject of vigorous debate within the IETF community. The aim is to clarify the ambiguities that led to those debates and to amplify the policy, in order to clarify what the IETF is currently doing.

The definitions matter for the rest of the document. An IETF Contribution is any submission to the IETF intended by the contributor for publication as all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, except for RFC Editor Contributions, and any statement made within the context of an IETF activity. That includes oral statements in IETF sessions and written and electronic communications made at any time or place, addressed to the IETF plenary session, any IETF working group or portion of it, the IESG or any member on behalf of the IESG, the IAB or any member on behalf of the IAB, any IETF mailing list, or the RFC Editor or the Internet-Drafts function. Statements made outside an IETF session, mailing list or other function that are clearly not intended to be input to an IETF activity are not IETF Contributions. An Internet-Draft is a temporary document used in the IETF and RFC Editor processes, posted on the IETF web site with a nominal maximum lifetime in the Secretariat's public directory of 6 months, after which it is removed. An RFC Editor Contribution is an Internet-Draft intended for publication as an Informational or Experimental RFC but not intended to be part of the IETF Standards Process. A Contributor is an individual submitting a Contribution.

The memo also lists the categories the rights fall into: rights to make use of contributed material, copyrights in IETF documents, rights to produce derivative works, and rights to use trademarks. It notes that a companion document, RFC 3979, deals with rights in technologies developed or specified as part of the IETF Standards Process, and that this document is not intended to address those issues. It says it is not intended as legal advice.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost anything you say or write in an IETF meeting, on an IETF mailing list, or in a draft counts as a contribution. By making one, you agree to give the IETF the rights it needs to publish and revise the work, and you confirm that the work contains nothing confidential. Everything else stays yours.

sections.title: The Rights an IETF Contribution Grants
sections.content:
The general policy in all matters of copyright and document procedures is that the intent is to benefit the Internet community and the public at large, while respecting the legitimate rights of others. On confidentiality, no information or document subject to any requirement of confidentiality or any restriction on its dissemination may be submitted as a Contribution or otherwise considered in any part of the IETF Standards Process, and there must be no assumption of any confidentiality obligation with respect to any Contribution. Each Contributor agrees that any statement in a Contribution, whether generated automatically or otherwise, stating or implying that the Contribution is confidential or subject to any privilege can be disregarded for all purposes and will be of no force or effect.

By submission of a Contribution, each person actually submitting it, and each named co-Contributor, is deemed to agree to the terms and to grant the following rights, on their own behalf and on behalf of the organization they represent or are sponsored by. To the extent that the Contribution or any portion of it is protected by copyright and other rights of authorship, they grant a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide right and license to the ISOC and the IETF under all intellectual property rights in the Contribution.

  • To copy, publish, display, and distribute the Contribution as part of the IETF Standards Process or in an Internet-Draft.
  • To prepare or allow the preparation of translations of the Contribution into languages other than English.
  • Unless explicitly disallowed in the notices contained in the Contribution, to prepare derivative works other than translations that are based on or incorporate all or part of the Contribution, or to comment upon it, within the IETF Standards Process. That licence grants the ISOC and the IETF no more rights than the licence to the original Contribution.
  • To reproduce any trademarks, service marks or trade names included in the Contribution solely in connection with the reproduction, distribution or publication of the Contribution and its derivative works. When reproducing Contributions, the IETF will preserve trademark and service mark identifiers used by the contributor, including (TM) and (R) where appropriate.
  • To extract, copy, publish, display, distribute, modify and incorporate into other works, for any purpose and not limited to use within the IETF Standards Process, any executable code or code fragments included in any IETF Document, such as MIB and PIB modules, subject to the requirements of Section 5, and on the understanding that this does not grant any right under any patent, patent application or other similar intellectual property right disclosed by the contributor under RFC 3979.

The Contributor also grants the IETF and ISOC permission to reference the name and address of the contributors and of the organizations they represent or are sponsored by.

Each Contributor represents, to the best of their knowledge and ability, that the Contribution properly acknowledges all major Contributors, where a major Contributor is any person who has materially or substantially contributed to it; that no information in the Contribution is confidential and that the IETF, ISOC and its affiliated organizations may freely disclose any information in it; that there are no limits to the Contributor's ability to make the grants, acknowledgments and agreements set out, that are reasonably and personally known to the Contributor; that the Contributor has not intentionally included material which is defamatory, untrue, or illegal under the laws of the jurisdiction in which the Contributor has their principal place of business or residence; and that all trademarks, trade names, service marks and other proprietary names used in the Contribution that are reasonably and personally known to the Contributor are clearly designated as such where reasonable. The Contributor and each named co-Contributor acknowledge that the IETF has no duty to publish or otherwise use or disseminate any Contribution, and that the IETF reserves the right to withdraw or cease using any Contribution that does not meet these requirements.

Contributors who claim trademark rights in terms used in their contributions are requested to state specifically what conditions apply to implementers of the technology relative to the use of those trademarks, submitted in the same way as other intellectual property claims.
sections.plainLanguage: Submitting a document is taken as agreeing to a licence. The licence is perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free and world-wide, and it covers copying, publishing, translating, making revised versions inside the IETF process, and reproducing any trademark. The author also promises that the document names everyone who contributed to it, that nothing in it is secret, and that they are allowed to give the licence.

sections.title: RFC Editor Contributions
sections.content:
Some drafts are not part of the IETF Standards Process. An RFC Editor Contribution is an Internet-Draft intended by the contributor to be submitted to the RFC Editor for publication as an Informational or Experimental RFC but not intended to be part of the IETF Standards Process. Because the IETF acts as publisher of Internet-Drafts even for drafts that are not intended to become part of the Standards Process, extra requirements apply to these documents.

All RFC Editor Contributions must meet the requirements of the general policy, the confidentiality obligations, the representations and warranties, the no duty to publish rule and the trademark provisions. Their grant of rights differs in one important respect. The Contributor grants a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide right and license to the ISOC and the IETF for at least the life of the Internet-Draft. The same four rights follow: to copy, publish, display and distribute the Contribution as an Internet-Draft, to prepare or allow the preparation of translations, to prepare derivative works other than translations unless explicitly disallowed in the notices, and to reproduce trademarks, service marks and trade names solely in connection with the reproduction, distribution or publication of the Contribution and its derivative works. The permission to reference the name and address of the contributors is granted in the same way.

What the RFC Editor Contribution does not carry is the fifth permission, the one that lets the IETF extract executable code and code fragments from an IETF Document and use them for any purpose.

Section 6 lists the notices and rights required in RFC Editor Contributions. Each must carry an IPR Disclosure Acknowledgement, identical to the one in Section 5.1, and one of three copyright release statements: that the author accepts the provisions of Section 3 of BCP 78, that the author accepts the provisions of Section 4 of BCP 78, or the Copyright Notice from Section 5.4 together with the disclaimer from Section 5.5. The RFC Editor may require additional notices.
sections.plainLanguage: A draft that is going to be published as an Informational or Experimental RFC rather than as part of the standards process gets a smaller set of rights, and the licence lasts only as long as the draft does. The one thing it does not get is permission to reuse the code in it.

sections.title: Notices Required in IETF Documents
sections.content:
The IETF requires that certain notices and disclaimers be reproduced verbatim in all IETF Documents, including copies, derivative works and translations, subject to the limited exceptions in Section 5.2. This requirement protects the IETF and its participants from liabilities connected with these documents. The copyright notice also alerts readers that the document is an IETF Document and that ISOC claims copyright rights to certain aspects of it, such as its layout, the RFC numbering convention and the prefatory language. That legend is not intended to imply that ISOC has obtained ownership of the IETF Contribution itself, which is retained by the authors or remains in the public domain as applicable.

Five notices are required or permitted. The IPR Disclosure Acknowledgement, in Section 5.1, is required in all Internet-Drafts and states that by submitting the Internet-Draft, each author represents that any applicable patent or other IPR claims of which he or she is aware have been or will be disclosed, and any of which he or she becomes aware will be disclosed, in accordance with Section 6 of BCP 79.

The Derivative Works Limitation, in Section 5.2, is for specific IETF Documents only. If the contributor wants to remove the IETF's right to make modifications and derivative works other than translations, one of two notices may be included in the Status of Memo section of an Internet-Draft and in a published RFC: that the document may not be modified and derivative works may not be created except to publish it as an RFC and to translate it, or that the document may not be modified and derivative works may not be created. In the case of MIB or PIB modules, and other cases where the Contribution includes material meant to be extracted for use, the statement other than to extract section XX as-is for separate use should be appended. Notice 5.2(a) is used if the contributor intends the Contribution to be published as an RFC. Notice 5.2(b) is used with the Publication Limitation when the contributor does not intend it to be published as an RFC. These notices may not be used with any standards-track document or with most working group documents, because the IETF must retain change control over its documents and the ability to augment, clarify and enhance the original Contribution in accordance with the IETF Standards Process. Notice 5.2(a) may be appropriate when republishing standards produced by other standards organizations, industry consortia or companies, which are typically published as Informational RFCs.

The Publication Limitation, in Section 5.3, is for specific types of Internet-Drafts only. If the contributor only wants the Contribution made available in an Internet-Draft, the notice This document may only be posted in an Internet-Draft may be included in the Status of Memo section. It can be used on Contributions intended to provide background information to educate and facilitate discussions within working groups but not to be published as RFCs.

The Copyright Notice, in Section 5.4, is required for all IETF Documents and is normally placed at the end of the document. It reads that the document is subject to the rights, licenses and restrictions contained in BCP 78, and that except as set forth therein, the authors retain all their rights. Additional copyright notices are not permitted in IETF Documents, except where the document is the product of a joint development effort between the IETF and another standards development organization, or is a republication of the work of another standards organization, and such exceptions must be approved on an individual basis by the IAB.

The Disclaimer, in Section 5.5, is required in all IETF Documents and is normally placed after the copyright notice. It states that the document and the information in it are provided on an AS IS basis and that the contributor, the organization represented, the Internet Society and the Internet Engineering Task Force disclaim all warranties, express or implied, including any warranty that use of the information will not infringe any rights or any implied warranties of merchantability or fitness for a particular purpose.

Section 5.6 sets out the exceptions. In MIB modules, PIB modules and similar material commonly extracted from IETF Documents, except for material placed under IANA maintenance, an abbreviated notice may be included in the body of the material in place of the notices required by Section 5. For example, that the version of the module is part of RFC XXXX and that one should see the RFC itself for full legal notices. Variations of these abbreviated notices are not permitted, except in joint development or republication cases approved individually by the IAB. Short excerpts of IETF Documents presented in electronic help systems, for example the DESCRIPTION clauses for MIB variables, do not need to include a copyright notice.
sections.plainLanguage: Every IETF document has to carry the same set of notices, word for word, so that the IETF is covered against claims arising from the documents it publishes. The notices say who owns the copyright, that the material comes with no warranty, and that the author has disclosed any patents they know about. A contributor can add a notice that stops the IETF from producing revised versions of the work, and one that stops the document being published as an RFC at all.

sections.title: Why the Rules Are the Way They Are
sections.content:
The memo explains the reasoning behind the provisions. A primary objective of the policy is to obtain from the document authors only the non-exclusive rights that are needed to develop and publish IETF Documents and to use the Contributions in the IETF Standards Process, while leaving all other rights with the authors. The non-exclusive rights the IETF needs are five: the right to publish the document, the right to let it be freely reproduced in the formats the IETF publishes it in, the right to let third parties translate it into languages other than English, except where explicitly excluded, the right to make derivative works within the IETF process, and the right to let third parties extract some logical parts, for example MIB modules. The authors retain all other rights but cannot withdraw these from the IETF and ISOC.

Because copyright rights come into existence whenever a work of authorship is created, and the IETF cannot make use of Contributions if it does not have sufficient rights in them, it is important that the IETF receive assurances from all Contributors that they have the authority to grant the rights they claim to grant. Without this assurance, the IETF and its participants would run a greater risk of liability to the owners of those rights. The assurances are requested only to the extent of the Contributor's reasonable and personal knowledge. That wording indicates that an organization cannot purposely keep an individual in the dark about patents or patent applications just to avoid the disclosure requirement, but it should not be interpreted as requiring a Contributor to perform a patent search.

On derivative works, the IETF needs to be able to evolve its documents in response to experience gained in deployment, to incorporate developments in research, and to react to changing conditions on the Internet. The right is required for all IETF standards track documents and most non-standards track documents, with two exceptions: documents describing proprietary technologies, and documents that are republications of the work of other standards organizations. A contributor who does not want to grant publication or derivative work rights before finding out whether a Contribution has been accepted for development may include the Derivative Works Limitation and the Publication Limitation in it. A working group can then discuss the draft, and if the Contribution is accepted for development the contributor must resubmit it without the limitation notices before the working group can formally adopt it as a working group document.

On trademarks, the IETF makes no judgment about the validity of any trademark rights, but requires each contributor to grant it a perpetual license to use such trademarks or service marks solely in exercising its rights to reproduce, publish and modify the Contribution. That license does not authorize any IETF participant to use a trademark in connection with any product or service offering, but only in the context of IETF Documents and discussions. The licenses are granted to all individuals noted in the definition of the IETF, irrespective of their employment or institutional affiliation, but they do not extend broadly to the employers, sponsors or institutions of those individuals.

Finally, some documents, including those produced by the U.S. government and those in the public domain, may not be protected by the same copyright and legal rights as other documents. Even so, the memo asks each contributor to grant the same rights and make the same representations as though the Contribution were protected, and asks for those grants only to the extent that the Contribution may be protected. The reason given is that they are necessary to protect the ISOC, the IETF, the IETF Standards Process and all participants, and because the IETF does not have the resources to make any independent investigation into the actual proprietary status of a submitted document.
sections.plainLanguage: The short version of the reasoning: the IETF only asks for the five things it actually needs, namely publishing, reproducing, translating, revising inside the process, and letting people lift out parts such as MIB modules. Everything else stays with the author. The assurance the author gives is about what they know, not about a search they have to run.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states that it relates to IETF process, not to any particular technology. There are security considerations when adopting any technology, but it says there are no known issues of security with IETF Contribution rights policies.
sections.plainLanguage: These are rules about paper, not about networks, so the memo says there are no known security issues with them.

viz.caption: THE NOTICES THAT IETF DOCUMENTS CARRY

items.title: IPR Disclosure Acknowledgement
items.text: Required in all Internet-Drafts. The author represents that any applicable patent or other IPR claims known to them have been or will be disclosed, in accordance with Section 6 of BCP 79.

items.title: Derivative Works Limitation
items.text: For specific IETF Documents only. Stops the IETF from making modified or derivative versions of the contribution.

items.title: Publication Limitation
items.text: For specific types of Internet-Drafts only. States that the document may only be posted as an Internet-Draft.

items.title: Copyright Notice
items.text: Required for all IETF Documents, normally at the end. The document is subject to BCP 78 and the authors retain all their rights.

items.title: Disclaimer
items.text: Required in all IETF Documents, normally after the copyright notice. The material is provided as is, with all warranties disclaimed.

viz.caption: THE FIVE NON-EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS THE IETF ASKS FOR

items.title: Publish
items.text: The right to publish the document.

items.title: Reproduce
items.text: The right to let the document be freely reproduced in the formats the IETF publishes it in.

items.title: Translate
items.text: The right to let third parties translate it into languages other than English.

items.title: Revise
items.text: Except where explicitly excluded, the right to make derivative works within the IETF process.

items.title: Extract
items.text: The right to let third parties extract some logical parts, for example MIB modules.
